pageProps.title: Murder on the Orient Express
pageProps.review: A review of Agatha Christie's representative mystery novel where Hercule Poirot uncovers the truth among 12 suspects with perfect alibis in a closed train, posing a heavy question about the legitimacy of private justice and righteousness.
pageProps.description: Facing a once-in-a-lifetime choice between legal justice and human justice
pageProps.content:
## Review A representative work featuring ```Hercule Poirot```, where a murder case occurs inside a train, a completely ```closed space```.
There is no trace of intrusion by an outsider, and 12 suspects are interrogated in turn, but all suspects have perfect alibis where they serve as each other's witnesses. And at the crime scene, only contradictory clues are found, such as a handkerchief with no owner, a pipe cleaner, and even twelve stab wounds of varying strength and depth. The case seemed to fall into a labyrinth due to the suspects' perfect alibis and the unnatural murder scene, but eventually, Poirot reveals the whole truth.
But Poirot finishes the case while hiding the truth.
While perfectly betraying the reader's expectations, it elevates the story to a deep dimension beyond the question of ```Whodunit``` to Whydunit (why did they have to become the culprits?).
If the law does not fulfill its role, can an individual directly executing justice truly be justified?
